overview:
The fighting that consumed most of the world between 1939 and 1945 grew out of two separate crises that eventually merged. In East Asia, Japan had been at war in China since 1937, driving deep into the country's heartland; in Europe, Nazi Germany spent the late 1930s dismantling the postwar settlement piece by piece while Britain and France tried to buy peace with concessions. The conventional starting date is 1 September 1939, when Germany invaded Poland and Britain and France declared war two days later, with the Soviet Union invading Poland from the east on 17 September under the terms of its pact with Hitler. Historians of Asia often push the start back to 1937, and the choice is not merely bookkeeping — it changes whose war this was and how long it lasted.

The first two years belonged to the Axis. Germany overran Denmark, Norway, the Low Countries and France in a matter of weeks in 1940, forcing the British evacuation from Dunkirk; the Royal Air Force then held off the Luftwaffe over southern England through that summer and autumn. In 1941 the war became genuinely global: Germany invaded Greece and Yugoslavia in the spring, turned east against the Soviet Union in June, and in December Japan struck Pearl Harbor and swept through Southeast Asia, taking Singapore in February 1942 in what remains one of the worst defeats in British military history. Under cover of this expansion the Nazi regime carried out the systematic murder of roughly six million Jews, alongside the killing of Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, Poles and others — genocide and conquest were bound together rather than incidental to each other. The tide turned across 1942 and 1943 at Stalingrad, at Midway, in the Anglo-American landings in North Africa and then Sicily, and at Kursk, where the largest armoured battle of the war ended Germany's ability to mount a strategic offensive in the east.

From there the Allies closed in from every direction, though slowly and at enormous cost. The Normandy landings opened a western front in June 1944; the same summer, a conspiracy of German officers tried and failed to kill Hitler in the 20 July plot, and the Polish Home Army rose in Warsaw only to be crushed over sixty-three days while the Red Army halted on the far bank of the Vistula. In the Pacific, the American victory at Leyte Gulf in October 1944 effectively destroyed the Japanese navy, and the battle for Okinawa in the spring of 1945 killed perhaps a third of the island's civilian population. Germany surrendered in May 1945; Japan capitulated in August after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet entry into the Pacific war. Estimates of the dead range from about 50 to 75 million or more, the great majority of them civilians, with the Soviet Union and China absorbing more than half the total.
significance: Almost every structure of the second half of the twentieth century was poured into the mould this war left behind. It ended European global primacy and replaced it with two nuclear-armed superpowers whose confrontation shaped the next four decades; it broke the prestige of the colonial empires in Asia badly enough that decolonisation became a matter of when rather than whether; and it produced the United Nations, the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals, the Genocide Convention and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the first serious attempt to make aggression and mass atrocity into crimes an individual could be tried for. It also normalised things that had once been unthinkable — the deliberate bombing of cities, industrialised killing, the mobilisation of entire societies — and left a set of borders, alliances and unresolved grievances, from divided Korea to the map of central Europe, that are still being argued over.
coverage: Written from general reference works (Wikipedia, Britannica), the US Holocaust Memorial Museum's treatment of the war in Europe, and the National WWII Museum's casualty tables; an Imperial War Museums page on the war's legacy would not load. The dataset's 312 events lean heavily toward European and Anglo-American military operations, so campaigns in China, Burma and the Dutch East Indies, occupation and resistance outside Europe, and civilian experience generally are thinly represented here relative to their weight in the war. The casualty figures are genuinely uncertain rather than merely rounded — Chinese and Soviet totals vary by many millions between sources, Japanese records were destroyed in 1945, and Soviet-era counts were political documents as much as demographic ones.
